As they do each year, Amazon’s book editors have selected the best books of the year across all genres, including their top 20 overall. Some you’ve probably heard of and others may have slipped your notice until now, but here are their very top 10 for your consideration before year’s end.

It has been revealed that “An extraordinary Trojan horse of a novel that will make your heart sing and make you want to talk to everybody you know about it. Utterly magnetic, American Hagwon will change the way you think about family, sacrifice, and education. Min Jin Lee has written (another) once-in-a-lifetime read.” —Al Woodworth, Amazon Editor.

Devastated by a shocking betrayal, John and Helen Koh move their three children from Seoul to Southern California. Fresh opportunity is everywhere for the children, while the elder Kohs find their education and experience in Korea does not translate to the States. As their friends, relatives, and enemies come and go, the family continues “nursing the almost all-consuming faith that education will lead the next generation to success and security.”.

Recent findings suggest that “A sparkling, genre-busting gift of a novel, Emily St. John Mandel’s latest is dystopian fiction that shook me to my core. Spanning continents, timelines, and perhaps even universes, Exit Party makes for a glorious puzzle, one with pieces that fit together seamlessly.” —Annabel Gutterman, Amazon Editor.

Sources indicate that scary Mommy editor Katie Garrity called this novel “mind-bending.” Set in 2031, California has declared itself a republic apart from the U.S. The curfew in Los Angeles lifts for the first time in weeks, and citizens gravitate to a big party. What happens there will haunt Ari Waker, freshly out of prison after 18 years, for years to come.

It has been revealed that “Robert Kolker’s enthralling medical mystery is both mesmerizing and heartbreaking — it asks big questions about chance and choice, what makes a full life, what we’re willing to run toward (or hide from), and how we care for each other. It’s a true story that will stick with you.” —Lindsay Powers, Amazon Editor.

Industry observers note that this is the heartbreaking true story of a family plagued by dementia as early as in their 40s due to a shared genetic mutation. In a family with nine siblings that all strike out as young adults, only the youngest child, Barb, is still home to see her mother become withdrawn and uncaring. Then, one by one, other members of the family begin losing jobs, destroying their marriages, and getting further and further away from their former selves. And it’s Barb who sets out to find answers — and a cure.”.

According to recent reports, “This was our pick for the best book of the year so far, and our love for this novel about two motherless friends coming of age in the Jim Crow South endures. A nuanced portrait of friendship, family, and race—Jones's sentences sing.” —Erin Kodicek, Amazon Editor.

If you love Jones’ previous work, you will not be disappointed by Kin, mentioned Scary Mommy editor Sarah Aswell after reading the book in July. It follows Annie and Vernice, who have been best friends and neighbors since they were kids in Honeysuckle, Louisiana. Then, at 18, Vernice heads for Spelman College where she is pulled into a world of aspiration and connection, while Annie sets out into the world to find love and adventure. Where will their journeys take them, and will they come back to each other?

“Walking the line between hysterical and horrifying, this electric psychological thriller ruthlessly takes on cultural appropriation through a delicious cat-and-mouse game like no other. If you’re in a reading slump, Fruit Fly is the cure.” —Abby Abell, Amazon Editor.

According to recent reports, mallory Maddox is a washed-up author who hasn’t put out fresh work in nearly a decade. All the buzz she worked so hard to earn is fading, and fast. So when she meets Leo, an unhoused addict trading sex for the things he needs, she finds her inspiration. How far will she go to write the perfect, career-saving story?”.

According to recent reports, “Never before have a 19th-century mapmaker, a scruffy, loyal dog, and a mysterious copse of trees been more enchanting. O’Farrell delivers a soaring and bewitching tale of family, and how the remote Irish peninsula where they live defines and shapes them, generation after generation.” —Al Woodworth, Amazon Editor.

Scary Mommy editor Sarah Aswell read Land in September and declared this story, about a family surviving Ireland’s Great Hunger who find a mysterious spring in the forest, may be O’Farrell’s best work yet.

“Illuminating and unforgettable, Patrick Radden Keefe’s latest delivers another knockout work of narrative nonfiction, this time telling the shocking story of how a young man got caught up in the dangerous and powerful world of Russian oligarchs and landed at the bottom of the Thames.” —Al Woodworth, Amazon Editor.

According to recent reports, if you love documentaries and true crime podcasts, this book is a must-read. In the wee hours of the morning of November 29, 2019, cameras outside MI6 headquarters captured footage of a young man pacing back and forth before throwing himself into the river Thames. What follows is a deeply reported account of his parents’ quest to get answers about what happened to their son, and how on earth he ended up deciding to jump.

“The many fans of Big Little Lies will love this follow-up, but you don’t need to have read that book or seen the show to enjoy Big Little Truths. I’ve been a fan of Liane Moriarty since her early books, and this is simply one of her very best. The dialogue is so clever, and the storytelling so engrossing, you won’t be able to put this book down.” —Sarah Gelman, Editorial Director.

Sources indicate that here’s how Scary Mommy editor Katie Garrity summed up the book after reading it in August: “Big Little Truths picks up 10 years later with Madeline, Celeste, Jane, Renata, and Bonnie, whose kindergartners are now teenagers navigating drugs, sex, and alcohol, which honestly sounds just as chaotic and stressful as the original but make it high school. When a mysterious stranger starts lurking around the school and the principal receives a severed finger in the mail, old secrets resurface and upcoming ones threaten to unravel everything.”.

“This heart-pounding, reported memoir sucked me in from the first page; it’s a gripping account of resilience and perseverance that goes far beyond the headlines to reveal what really happened to Evan Gershkovich when he was snatched off the street and thrown into a Russian prison.” —Lindsay Powers, Amazon Editor.

It has been revealed that in March 2023, one year after Russia invaded Ukraine, journalist Evan Gershkovich met with a source roughly 900 miles east of Moscow. Out of nowhere, a group of masked agents bursts in, blindfolds him, and abducts him. They tell him he’s being charged as a spy before dumping him in Lefortovo prison. Instead of giving up, Evan kept reporting, all the way up until the prisoner swap that set him free.

“Two-time Pulitzer Prize winner Colson Whitehead delivers another searing page-turner of heists, gangsters, criminals, and families in this mesmerizing portrait of 1980s New York City.” —Al Woodworth, Amazon Editor.

If you love a good crime novel, don’t skip Cool Machine. It follows Ray Carney, his wife Elizabeth, and partner Pepper through years of heists, body guard gigs, and major transitions in New York’s history. At every turn he comes up against the most violent forces in the city, risking the safety of himself and his family for one more score.

Which of these books just moved straight to the top of your TBR?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

America’s dad has a very pointed and personal message.

Sources indicate that let’s be honest, Ty Burrell, aka Phil Dunphy from Modern Family, could give us a good talking to about the finer points of latex paint and we’d probably cozy up to listen. He’s just that kind of guy — disarmingly affable and sincere and funny. This is a good thing because right now he’s talking about meningitis. Yes, meningitis, that overlooked infection that, you probably didn’t know, kills 1 in 10 who develop it with 1 in 5 having long-term health consequences like brain damage and hearing loss. Also, kids age 16 to 23 have the highest rates of it. And that’s what brings us here with Burrell, a dad of two teens, and a message. In partnership with GSK (for the Ask2BSure campaign) Burrell has teamed up once again with Julie Bowen and a stand-in teen actor (mom and dad are back!) to give awareness and, yes, make jokes.

Leading up to the campaign we talked to Burrell about his own two teens and how’s he’s doing as a parent of a notoriously tough age, what advice he has for those with pre-teens, and how he’s become the doorjamb of the family (and that’s ok!).

So … Why are you, Ty Burrell, America’s dad, talking about meningitis?

Sources indicate that well, it's pretty organic, actually. I have teenage girls, and unfortunately, the most vulnerable population is, actually, I guess, teens to college, 16 to 23. And that's doing large part to the teen lifestyle. My girls play sports, and there's a lot of water bottle swapping. And once you're in college, it's dorm rooms and it's kissing and all of it. And there's a lot of bugs that go around in that environment.

According to recent reports, but meningitis doesn't come up as often as I think it really should, because I know there was just a recent outbreak in Britain, and there's the potential for long-term effects, and sometimes, unfortunately, death. I think one in five who get it have lifelong effects like limb loss and brain damage, loss of sight, and then one in ten die. So that's why I'm partnering with GSK on the Ask2BSure campaign to raise awareness about meningococcal disease or meningitis.

To that end, we made a video that we hope is funny, kind of a lighthearted way to educate people and inform people.

It is funny! But I must say as a parent of a 14-year-old, I almost couldn't get the humor because I got afraid.

Industry observers note that yeah, I know. It's a tightrope walk, isn't It?

According to recent reports, I happened to have a doctor check in with my 14-year-old this week and I asked them about meningitis. It turns out that I'm two years early. So I'm wondering outside of this PSA, which I think will get people asking doctors, what basic things should parents of teens know.

Well, I would direct them to a healthcare professional in terms of all of the basics. But what I know is that the vaccines available, in terms of strains, A, B, C, W, and Y, but a lot of teens don't have the meningitis B vaccination. And that was true of my 16-year-old. And I did the same thing. When I started to learn more about how serious this was, I had a conversation with our doctor and she hadn't had B yet, so that's now scheduled. And I mean, as far as my knowledge about it, it would be that and really just encouraging people to have a conversation with their doctor about the risks of meningitis and about vaccination, and if that's an option.

In a recent development, it is that simple. I was wondering, I mean, we dads, are always look for a way to make something into a lecture... Is there a way to segue from the meningitis talk or explanation to other necessary talks?

You do have to say it's because you're probably going to be making out with people.

Yeah, totally. I don't know what it's like for you, but I feel like the window in which I actually have any influence for them is three sentences. And I don't know if that's a lack of attention span because of phones or screens or what have you, or it's just time-honored parenting, that you just have the floor for a brief moment before you are tuned out.

Recent findings suggest that “This very hard for me because I want to be my kid's best friend. This is where I share personality traits with Phil Dunphy.”.

And their brains short-circuit.

Industry observers note that totally. And get frustrated fast. It's a lecture. We're now in a lecture. So I don't know about the segueing into a separate topic, but I will say that my wife, luckily, with girls is taking the conversation off of my plate.

Oh great. You can just tell them how dirty dorm rooms are.

That's the dad's role. So you have two teens now. What's the toughest things you've found about raising them and maybe what's the best?

I think that the really natural want for independence, especially our 16-year-old ... Well, actually both of them, we have a 16 and a 14-year-old, but I think they are both craving more independence and more of their own choices and more of their own time. And yet we're still on the job. We are the ones that have to keep them healthy and safe. And so I feel like, I don't know if you feel this way, but I feel like the challenge is really making them feel heard and seen and giving them as much freedom as I possibly can. And still, which it's hard to do because once they experience some of that freedom, it's very hard for them to then have you say, "But not this thing, that's dangerous," or, "That's unhealthy," or whatever that is.

In a recent development, this is why, and this is very hard for me because I want to be my kid's best friend. This is where I share personality traits with Phil Dunphy. I really want to be their friend, but you really can't ... It's not always an option. It just isn't always an option. A lot of points, you have to actually say, "No, you are going to be mad at me, but this is about health and safety." That's the hardest thing. And then I think added on to that, it's like how do you remain connected to them in a time when they're trying to find their own voice and trying to separate from you really? And I think that's completely natural. They are actually trying to pull away so they can be their own selves, and yet it's really key, I think, that you stay connected. I got really good advice from this book a long time ago called The Wonder of Girls, and his advice was like, "They're going to be really mean to you, and don't take it personally." He remarked, "Just stay nearby. Don't take it personally, be nearby." And that's always been in the back of my mind.

It has been revealed that metaphorically, I'm kind of by the doorjamb of the room. Are you thirsty? Everything okay in there? You safe? But yeah, it's not easy.

That's Great. The Go the F*ck to Sleep author just wrote an essay for Fatherly for his latest book Go to the F*ck to College ...

Oh, I didn't know there was a sequel.

Sources indicate that it just came out! It should be very pertinent to you. But he talks about one piece advice he got from a friend was all teens are saying, "F*ck you, tuck me in. " And I think it's just a more crude way of saying what you were just saying.

Industry observers note that it kind of covers it. I still get requests. My daughter will act like she never wants to see me again, and then I'll hear like, "Are you not tucking me in? " Okay, I guess there's something there still.

So what's the best part of raising a teen? For the preteen parents in our audience, can you give them some hope — and maybe advice?

According to recent reports, I would say the level of nuance in conversation is a real high for me, especially somebody who is interested in comedy. My 16-year-old is pretty stoic. I always think of her as the leading man in a Western or something. She's this person staring off distance, and she's got three words for any answer. But my 14-year-old has always had a strong sense of irony, always, always been funny, and always had a real sense of looking at the world and seeing irony. And as she gets older, her perspective on things, it's pretty remarkable to be around a kid who is starting to see the world and seeing some of the contradictions of the world and some of the things that are unfair, but also just the things that are inherently funny about how seriously we all take ourselves. It's pretty cool. So I think that's one of the great trade-offs is that you end up actually having an intimate relationship with somebody who is really experiencing some of these perspectives for the first time.

That's great. And then any advice for our younger audience? I mean, as far as parenting advice, but also you were thinking about meningitis, any just really pragmatic pitfalls that you would've done differently?

I would say if I were going to go back and re-parent, I would say, "Bend, don't break." I would've given them both more of a leash. Leash is a terrible word for kids really, but you know what I mean? More slack in terms of just they're really exploring who they are and letting them really ... I think we did our best with that, but you're so worried about health and safety, that is mental health, physical health. I think that's a substantial part of why the meningitis, this campaign to talk about it is really vital to me because at the very end of the day, that is the bottom line. No matter whether they consider me a friend or not, I do have to keep them safe. And we've already had lots of bugs go through the family from their interactions with other teens, including mono and all kinds of stuff. But if you get meningitis, that's a whole different ballgame.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Happy Father’s Day, from one cool dad to the next.

Industry observers note that if you follow Fatherly’s Instagram handle, you may notice that we’ve been talking to a number of cool dads lately. We start by asking them about some of the little things that bring us the most joy, like the best movie to watch with your kid (among the answers, The Princess Bride, Zootopia, Sketch, Hook), the clothing they’re passionate about (black t-shirts, black button downs, and Jordan 1s are popular) and the music we blast for our kids (from Michal Jackson to Nirvana, Chance the Rapper to The Lone Bellow).

But look past these small insights and you’ll find successful men who are eager to talk about their kids. The variety of responses show how every dad has their own take, their unique philosophy about being a good man, a strong partner, and a great parent. It also indicates how much solidarity there is in being a dad.

Max Holloway, the dominant UFC fighter states he believes in being strict, but “it’s not just me being hard on him and busting his chops, but also encouraging him and telling him he did a good job.”.

Tony Hale, who needs no introduction if you’re a fan of Toy Story, Arrested Development, or Veep, admits he was more of a helicopter parent, one whose kids—now in college—know that, "Hey, when you need me, I'm always going to be here.”.

Colton Underwood, the former reality star and pro football player is serious about the job: “I have the responsibility that he grows up to be a great human being that does good in the world.” While Maurice Edu, who you’ve no doubt been hearing calling the World Cup shots on Fox Sports, finds fatherhood to be fairly effortless because “I always knew I wanted to be a father, but until I actually became one, I didn't realize how much I wanted it.".

Minneapolis lawyer and former mayoral candidate Jazz Hampton believes that “Fatherhood is how you show up for your own kids and the rest of the world as well, and how you teach your kids to show up for other people.” Meanwhile, the “Tired Dad” Jon Gustin notes that parenting is tough, but rewarding — a “badge of honor that we wear because we're showing up in all areas.”.

Then there’s Tom Llamas, our latest Cool Dad and the anchor of "NBC Nightly News” and "Top Story with Tom Llamas" on NBC News NOW. In a recent chat, Llamas reminded me that we, dads who are parenting now in 2026, weren’t the first and won’t be the last. Our parents struggled and cared and went through it all with their kids, and so did their dads, and theirs before them.

Llamas’ father, a Cuban refugee and dentist, was a big role model to him. “I learned a lot of great lessons from my dad,” Llamas says, “and then also try to be a better dad, and I think that's what my dad tried to do, too. He had a good dad, but he tried to be a better dad, and I'm trying to do the same thing.”.

Sources indicate that tom Llamas’ parents fled Cuba for Florida during Fidel Castro’s takeover of the country. Years later, in 1979, Tom was born. Llamas remembers a childhood in Miami that was a stark contrast to life in Cuba, under the rule of a dictator in a harsh economic economic environment. Primarily, he remembers his parents being there for him. “They would close the office early, like when I had sports, you know, to go and see me. Or if I had a school event they would close the office early, and for a small business that's income that you're not bringing in.”.

Industry observers note that tom Llamas and family. Credit: NBC.

He continues, “I'm grateful to have parents that always supported me in whatever I wanted to do — whether it was playing sports as a little boy, or when I got into journalism, or when I was into speech and debate in high school, to helping me when I had internships, because back when I was an intern you would not get paid.”.

Sources indicate that llamas claims he now lives and breathes this family-first philosophy himself. The other night Llamas, who now lives in Fresh York, anchored from the World Cup in Los Angeles and went to the game. “But then that same night, I jumped on a red eye so I could be home for a 9 AM little league game, and that's not something that that anyone has to ask me for — that's something I want to do, because I just believe that that kind of stuff needs to be automatic.”.

According to recent reports, this Father’s Day, Llamas has a message for all the dads out there: “It is the best job in the world to be a father [but] give yourself some grace cause it's really tough out there. There's a lot of books and opinions and podcasts and all kinds of things that are trying to tell people how to [parent] and I think, you know, just enjoy your time with your kids. Because it goes by very fast, and I truly think the greatest thing in the world is to be a dad.”.

The perforated design helps your sponge dry quickly, while the open bottom means you can also use this for storing handled scrub brushes.

Sources indicate that building blocks have come a long way since most of us were kids, and this plant lovers set is the proof. Once assembled, you’ll be staring back at an amazing botanical scene. This tiny plants LEGO set is so cute that you’ll want to show it off to friends and family. With 758 pieces in a set, you’ll be building for hours.

Sources indicate that magnetic to stick to your vehicle, golf cart, or any metal surface around your home, this light is easily recharged via USB-C. Choose from various lighting modes: single flash, double flash, triple flash, penta flash, double-quadra flash, SOS, and white light mode. One reviewer wrote, “Very bright light. Almost blinding. Definitely visible at night from long distances. Perfect for putting on your car if you have to pull over on the side of the road. Everyone will see you from a mile away. Light works perfectly every time.”.

Turn almost any bottle into a night-light with this clever bottle stopper that doubles as a lamp. Simply insert the rubber-lined stopper to create an air-tight seal, then tap the top to adjust the color temperature and brightness. It conveniently charges via USB cable, making it easy to keep powered.

Now you can toss all those smelly, sweaty caps right into the washer when you use these hat cages. The washer-ready cage creates a protective layer around most-sized caps, helping them keep their shape while getting nice and clean. Just place a cap between the cage, clip it closed, and toss it in the wash.

In a recent development, water and your favorite coffee grinds are all that’s needed to make the perfect cup of joe when you use this ingenious portable coffee press. It’s easy to use and features a fine filter that ensures no bitterness or grit. And since it's compact and made from shatterproof Tritan, it’s ideal for taking on the go. One satisfied shopper gushed, “The AeroPress is absolutely worth the hype, especially if you’re picky and want one of the best (if not THE best) tasting brew you can make.”.

Turn any toilet into a bidet with this best-selling handheld sprayer kit. It’s quick and easy to install and clips right to the toilet tank for easy access (or mount it to the wall). Plus, it features an adjustable water pressure sprayer and a flexible braided stainless steel hose for added convenience and durability.

According to recent reports, resembling the moon with its minimalist build, this alarm clock will look stunning on your nightstand — but it does so much more than. With gentle wake-up lighting, 10 soothing nature sounds, and a night-light function, it will create a serene oasis. It has three adjustable brightness levels, a snooze function, and multiple atmospheric lighting options, too.

Sources indicate that make the most of unused space in your car with this stick-on seat organizer. Made from high-quality PU leather, it’s soft yet durable, with neat stitching and a waterproof, scratch-resistant finish. Mount it to seat seams or flat surfaces to store your phone, cards, glasses, receipts, or other small essentials. It’s an affordable and space-saving addition to any ride.

It has been revealed that made of pink Himalayan salt, this two-pound rock is designed to hang from your showerhead or tub’s tap. As water flows over it, it adds minerals to your water for a spa-like experience. It even comes with a mesh bag for hanging dry between uses. You can also soak it in the tub as desired.

Industry observers note that this squishy fidget toy has a soft, slow-rising texture that’s genuinely satisfying to squeeze. Use it to help clear and calm your mind through simple, repetitive motion. The elasticity makes it ideal for kneading during work, study, or downtime, offering a calming sensory outlet without screens or noise — and the butter scent is a fun bonus.

Recent findings suggest that an elevated version of your usual fridge magnets, this pack of eight looks like detailed leaves for a fresh and lively look. Four styles come included and they measure nearly 2 inches long. One shopper wrote, “These were a very pleasant surprise. The magnet on them, for its small size, is VERY strong. [...] These look so much better than the myriad of souvenir magnet I have collected over the years. The colors and detail are really life like, not cheap looking.”.

Designed for convenience, the mini torpedo level features strong magnets for hands-free use and LED-lit bubble vials that are easy to read in dim workspaces. It’s small enough to slip into a pocket or toolbox, and perfect for hanging pictures, aligning shelves, home renovation tasks, or DIY decorating. It’s a significant upgrade on traditional levels for a great price.

This roomy cat-shaped makeup bag keeps your everyday essentials contained without hogging counter space. The drawstring design opens wide so you can actually see what you packed, then cinches closed to keep your contents secure. Made from durable polyester with a playful 3D cat face, it’s a cheap, practical, and playful addition to your vanity, gym bag, or suitcase.

In a recent development, you can place your plant clippings in this four-vase propagation station and watch them thrive, even in low-light settings. That’s thanks to the integrated LED light strip that offers nine brightness settings. The durable beechwood design comes with an included USB port and charging cable to keep them juiced.

When your accessories should be just as fun as the outfit, reach for these LED scrunchies. They feature three light modes that glow, flash, or shine steadily, turning a simple ponytail or bun into a full-on statement. Soft yarn construction keeps them comfortable and breathable, while a woven texture helps the lights shine brighter for extra visual impact. Each set includes six scrunchies.

Life feeling like a dumpster fire? At least your writing utensils can match the mood when you have these ballpoint pens. Each one is topped with a mini dumpster fire with the message “I’m fine, it’s fine, everything is fine.” (Accurate.) And since 12 come in a pack, you can gift them to your coworkers, too.

Recent findings suggest that this night-light is more like a tiny, illuminated work of art. Featuring a vintage-inspired stained glass globe, it casts a colorful glow on the wall behind it. The stepless dimmer on the side lets you get bright light or soft, cozy illumination that’s perfect for midnight snack runs to the kitchen.

These toe separators create plenty of space to help you get a neat, smudge-free pedicure. But let’s not bury the lede — the, colorful flowery shapes give them the most whimsical look (you might just find yourself swapping shades midweek to use them again). Another bonus use? They can help stretch out your toes and alleviate discomfort after a day spent in tight shoes.

Recent findings suggest that got an old piece of furniture you’re tired of looking at? Swap in these crystal knobs to breathe newly introduced life into it. They have a gorgeous, gem-like design wrapped in copper wire, totally transforming even your most basic IKEA dresser. Choose from several shades including sapphire blue and emerald green.

According to recent reports, if your outdoor space is feeling lackluster in the evenings, it might be missing these solar-powered globe lights that create an instant cozy glow. The cracked glass surface feels vintage and magical, while the waterproof, weather-resistant design means you can leave them out even when the forecast calls for a downpour. Use them to line a walkway, to illuminate your patio table, or just scatter them around your garden.

Headrest hooks like these are an amazing way to keep purses and takeout bags up and off the floor (and not rolling around with every turn). This set takes things up a notch thanks to the pearl-dotted design that gives your interior some Chanel-inspired vibes. And though they look delicate, they can hold a hefty 44 pounds each.

It has been revealed that keeping your phone powered up in the car has never been easier... or more magical. This charger casts a starry projection on your car’s ceiling for a cool, galactic effect that you can turn off as needed. As for charging, you’ll get retractable Lightning and USB-C cables as well as two additional ports, making it easy to keep your devices juiced and ready to go.

Recent findings suggest that the genius design of this laundry bag allows you to compress dirty clothing towards the end of a trip, freeing up precious space in your luggage for souvenirs. It has a handle at the top for toting around, and a one-way valve on the bottom or squeezing out excess air as you compress — no vaccum required. The inside is waterproof for damp items and keeps smells locked within.

In a recent development, this tiny garden gnome is living his best life on his swing perch — and the adorable figurine comes with twine for you to hang it wherever it will deliver the most joy. Crafted from durable, weatherproof resin, it’s a piece of yard decor that will hold up season after season.

It has been revealed that fresh flowers are a vibe but they can fade and wilt fast. That’s where this tiny copper charm comes in handy. Drop it in and it helps keep water free of slime and ensures your flowers last longer. “It’s not only so beautiful, but it miraculously works! [...] I usually get 1 week at best with plant food. With [this charm] I got 3 weeks,” raved one fan. It comes with a small pouch for storage.

Industry observers note that enjoy a serene aquarium vibe without the commitment of an aquarium: This special lamp is filled with jellyfish that float and dance through the water (thanks to the small motor inside). It plugs in for power, and there’s a handy timer function.

Industry observers note that not only are these tea bag bookmarks cute and colorful, but they also offer a clever option for keeping your spot in your current read. The bag will secure in between the pages, and the string will hang out the top for spotting. Six come in a pack.

Break up a stressful workday by playing in this miniature turtle sandbox ... it’s surprisingly calming. Included are small accessories (like shovels and buckets) for even more fun. And the shell keeps it closed when not in use.

This power failure alarm will beep when a power outage is detected on an item like your fridge, sump pump, furnace, etc. It’s a must-have. The alarm can be set to five volume levels and seven sirens, ensuring you can always hear it.

It has been revealed that run one of these therapy brushes along your skin for a soothing massage. Each one (three come with) features tons of soft bristles to help, and the portable size means you can toss it in your bag.

In a recent development, this charming bird candle is made entirely from real paraffin wax, yet the flickering “flame” is completely fake. It’s battery powered so there’s no hazard involved. Display it proudly on your mantle, tablescape, and more.

It has been revealed that at-home pedicures are way easier to pull off with this foot rest that can be set to six different heights for adequate positioning. It’s nonslip, heavy duty (supporting up to 220 pounds), and folds flat for convenient storage.

In a recent development, effortlessly peel garlic with this clever three-pack of garlic skin removers. The textured inner surface gently grips garlic skin, peeling it away with each rolling motion. As one shopper explained, “Peeling garlic can be tedious. This little gadget is amazing. Clove is inserted into the peeler, a few rolls back and forth (I use the palm of my hand) and out comes a perfectly peeled clove of garlic. Best thing you didn’t know you needed.”.

It has been revealed that this vintage yet modern table lamp is entirely cordless, so you can move it with you from table to nightstand to desk, and back again. The rechargeable design has an incredibly long batter life, providing up to 13 days of light. With three color temperatures to choose from, it makes any room feel more elegant.

It has been revealed that these brass birds sit neatly on door hinge pins or attach to metal surfaces using discreet built-in magnets, adding a charming touch in unexpected places. Lightweight and easy to reposition, they can be placed on hinges, cabinets, shelves, picture frames, or any magnetic spot where you want a subtle upgrade. They’re the kind of decorative touch that shows your attention to detail. Each set comes with three birds.

35 Back-To-School Sports Gear Essentials Every Young Athlete Needs

📅 15 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3106 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From activewear to snacks to the crucial stuff we all forget about, here’s your complete product guide to the gear your young athlete needs.
  • According to recent reports, back-to-school season does not just mean notebooks, lunch boxes, and the shoes your kid insists everyone else already has.
  • Sources indicate that most young athletes need the same basic stuff, no matter what they play: a sturdy water bottle, sweat-ready clothes, socks that do not quit, sunscreen, towels, deodorant, recovery gear, and something to contain the mess.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From activewear to snacks to the crucial stuff we all forget about, here’s your complete product guide to the gear your young athlete needs.

According to recent reports, back-to-school season does not just mean notebooks, lunch boxes, and the shoes your kid insists everyone else already has. If your kid plays sports, it also means damp socks wedged into the back seat, a gym bag that smells like evidence, water bottles with no lids, and a towel that is wet, rank, and somehow still in use.

Sources indicate that most young athletes need the same basic stuff, no matter what they play: a sturdy water bottle, sweat-ready clothes, socks that do not quit, sunscreen, towels, deodorant, recovery gear, and something to contain the mess. Nothing here is precious. Nothing is so sport-specific that it only works for one season. This is the Amazon gear parents end up buying anyway, pulled together before the season takes over the sports bag, the laundry room, and your will to live.

A good water bottle is the first thing every young athlete needs, and the first thing they will leave on a bench somewhere. Look for one that is durable, easy to clean, and massive enough to get them through practice.

The 50-ounce size gives kids enough water for long practices and tournament days, and the tethered leakproof cap means one less loose lid rolling around the car. It is also lightweight, clippable, and dishwasher-safe, which matters because no parent needs another thing that requires special handling.

Some practices are long, hot, and sweaty enough that water alone may not cut it. A sports drink can help replace electrolytes when sweat is doing most of the work.

This variety pack has electrolytes, with no added sugar and no artificial sweeteners, flavors, or dyes. At 20 calories per bottle, it is a lighter sports-drink option for parents who want hydration help without sending a kid into practice with something that looks like melted candy.

Some sports days run straight through the normal eating schedule, which is how kids end up starving in the car and furious at everyone. A protein bar is useful before practice, after practice, or between games, but check school rules and allergens before tossing one into a team bag.

It has been revealed that this 10-count variety pack has flavors built around chocolate, peanut butter, blueberry, fruit, and nuts. The bars are gluten-free, made with simple ingredients, and have 12 grams of protein per bar, but some contain common allergens including eggs, peanuts, almonds, and cashews.

Sources indicate that fall sports still mean sun exposure. A sweat-resistant sunscreen belongs in every sports bag, especially for after-school practices, weekend tournaments and kids who swear they “don’t burn.”.

In a recent development, this sunscreen is fast-absorbing, nongreasy, and water- and sweat-resistant for up to 80 minutes, which makes it a practical fit for practices and games. Supergoop is made for face and body, so kids do not need separate bottles.

Industry observers note that A school backpack is already doing too much. A dedicated sports bag gives clothes, towels, water bottles, deodorant, and gear somewhere to live that is not the floor of your car.

This has a spacious main compartment for school and practice gear, plus a ventilated shoe compartment to keep wet sneakers or cleats away from clean clothes and tech. The water-resistant base is the quiet win here, because locker room floors, wet fields, and rainy parking lots are not kind to regular backpacks.

According to recent reports, wet socks, damp towels, and postpractice clothes should not touch anything clean. A wet-dry bag keeps the gross stuff contained until someone remembers laundry exists.

Industry observers note that these bags are technically built for diapers, swimsuits, and day care messes, which is exactly why it works for youth sports. The 12.5-by-16-inch size, washable fabric, heat-sealed seams, and leak-resistant design make it useful for wet socks, damp towels, and gear you do not want touching anything else.

Cotton is fine until it turns into a wet dish towel with sleeves. A moisture-wicking shirt helps kids stay more comfortable through practice, conditioning, and the ride home.

The quick-drying fabric wicks sweat and dries fast, which is the whole point of a practice shirt. It is soft enough for school or general wear too, so it does not become another piece of gear that only gets used once a week.

Every young athlete needs shorts that can handle sweat, dirt, turf, and repeated washing. They should be light, easy to move in, and not so expensive that losing one pair becomes a family event.

According to recent reports, the listing calls these soccer shorts, but the sweat-wicking Climacool fabric, adjustable drawcord waist, and recycled polyester interlock make them useful for more than one sport. They are built for movement and repeated washing, which is what matters.

Bad underwear can ruin a practice faster than bad weather. Athletic underwear should move, breathe, and stay put under uniforms, shorts, and base layers without bunching, pinching, or becoming the thing your kid complains about the entire ride home.

These have a 5-inch inseam, a wide soft waistband, a breathable athletic feel, and flatlock seams for durability. The contoured pouch and tagless back make them a practical under-uniform option for boys who need support without bulk.

These are made with smooth stretch fabric, a seamless waistband, and a tag-free design to help reduce irritation during school, sports, and everyday movement. The lightweight performance fabric gives active kids a flexible fit without pinching, digging, or bunching under gear.

A hoodie is the unofficial uniform of kids waiting before games, riding home after practice, or denying they are cold.

This is a straightforward school-to-practice hoodie with a relaxed fit, kangaroo pocket, thumbholes, and midweight fabric. It is the kind of layer kids can wear constantly without making you nervous every time it leaves the house.

A base layer helps with sweat, coverage, and comfort without adding bulk. It works under jerseys, hoodies, and uniforms when the weather cannot decide to be seasonally appropriate.

This long-sleeve top is made with lightweight HeatGear fabric that wicks sweat and dries fast, with mesh panels for ventilation and flatlock seams for easier movement. It is not a heavy thermal layer, but that is why it works for school sports: Kids can wear it under gear without overheating five minutes into warm-ups.

In a recent development, socks disappear faster than almost anything else in a young athlete’s life. Buy more than seems reasonable, because wet, thin, or blister-making socks can wreck a practice fast.

These socks use a combed cotton and polyester blend with spandex for stretch, which means they are built to breathe, hold their shape, and survive repeated washing. The medium cushioning and reinforced heels and toes make them a practical everyday pick for kids who burn through socks like it is part of the sport.

Sources indicate that slides give kids something easy to wear before and after games, especially when cleats are muddy, socks are wet, or feet need a break. They also make locker rooms, pools, and postpractice errands less gross.

These slides use OOfoam, which the brand notes absorbs 37% more impact than traditional footwear foams. The closed-cell foam is machine-washable and designed to minimize odor, which makes it perfect for locker rooms, postgame errands, and the ride home.

A quick-dry towel works for sweat, rain, swimming, muddy legs, and the towel situation no parent wants to inspect. It dries faster than a regular bath towel, which matters when it gets forgotten in a bag overnight.

The listing states it absorbs five times its own weight and dries fast when hung by the snap loop. It also packs into a ventilated carry bag, which makes it easier to keep in a sports bag than a bulky bath towel from home.

A sports bag becomes a swamp fast. Packing cubes give clean clothes, extra socks, base layers, and small gear a fighting chance of staying together instead of becoming part of the bottom-of-the-bag sludge.

It has been revealed that these packing cubes keep clean backup clothes, socks, and small gear organized inside a sports bag, backpack or a duffel. The Del Dia colors are random and one-of-a-kind, which means no two sets look the same, and your kid has a chance — albeit small — of recognizing their own stuff.

It has been revealed that youth sports shoes can turn toxic fast, especially when they live in a bag between practices. A shoe deodorizer helps keep sneakers, cleats, and slides from stinking up the car, mudroom, or whatever corner your kid has claimed for gear.

These compact deodorizers are built for shoes, gym bags, lockers, and sports gear, so they do not just solve one stink problem. The twist-to-activate design lets kids control the scent level, assuming they remember to use these before the shoes become a family problem.

According to recent reports, some sports smells do not come out in the wash because the offending item never goes in the wash. A gear spray helps with helmets, gloves, pads, bags, and other equipment that gets sweaty, rank, and somehow keeps getting used.

This spray deodorizes sports equipment, including helmets, gloves, bags, pads and gym gear, and the brand states it works for everything from football and hockey to lacrosse, soccer, volleyball, and boxing. It only requires a spray-and-air-dry routine, which is about as much cleaning as most sports families can promise on a weeknight.

Keep one in the sports bag, one at home, and maybe one in the car, because youth sports have a way of exposing every deodorant failure.

It has been revealed that this deodorant is dermatologically tested and made for young, sensitive skin, which makes sense for kids who are just starting to need it. It is designed to protect against body odor without using a grown-up scent that confirms itself from across the room.

In a recent development, sometimes there is no shower. Body wipes help kids clean up enough to survive the car ride, dinner, homework or whatever comes next.

In a recent development, these individually wrapped 8-by-10-inch wipes are made for the exact no-shower problem sports families know well. They are hypoallergenic, paraben-free, and alcohol-free, and include aloe vera and vitamin E, so they are a practical bag staple for postpractice cleanup.

Sources indicate that fields, gyms, locker rooms, and portable bathrooms are not exactly sterile environments. Hand sanitizer is small, cheap, and useful before snacks, after bathroom runs, and after handling shared gear.

This unscented trio gives you three travel-friendly sanitizer sprays, which is useful if you want one for the sports bag, one for the car, and one that will disappear immediately.

According to recent reports, sunscreen, deodorant, lip balm, wipes, hair ties, and sanitizer should not be rolling loose at the bottom of a sports bag. A small toiletry bag keeps the tiny essentials together and makes them easier to find.

Industry observers note that this zip pouch has internal mesh pockets and a separate compartment, so the small stuff has a fighting chance of staying organized. The swivel hook is useful for hanging it in a locker, on a backpack or anywhere that is not the bottom of a filthy sports bag.

According to recent reports, lips burn too, and kids almost never think about it. SPF lip balm is small enough to live in a bag and useful for long days outside.

In a recent development, this three-pack has SPF 30 and includes aloe and vitamin E to help protect and moisturize lips. The multi-pack is useful because lip balm has the life expectancy of a loose sock.

It has been revealed that late-summer and fall practices can come with mosquitoes, especially on fields near grass, water, or woods. Bug spray keeps kids from spending half of practice swatting instead of playing.

This spray repels mosquitoes, ticks, and biting flies, and the misting design gives more even coverage than the panic-spray method most kids use.

Sources indicate that hair ties vanish, break, and somehow become community property. Keep extras in the sports bag for any kid who needs hair out of their face, whether they play rec soccer or want to look like Norway’s Erling Haaland before warm-ups.

Recent findings suggest that these hair ties are designed to flex with different hair thicknesses and hold without pinching or pulling. They are also made to minimize breakage, which matters when a kid is ripping out a ponytail in the car after practice.

Fall sports do not stop because the weather is annoying. A lightweight rain jacket gives kids real coverage for wet practices, sidelines, and the long walk from field to car.

This waterproof nylon shell is light enough to layer but protective enough for everything from drizzle to a sudden downpour. It has a hood, two hand pockets, elastic cuffs, and reflective detail, which makes it a practical all-season piece for kids who will absolutely claim they are fine while visibly getting soaked.

It has been revealed that something will hurt. A reusable ice pack is useful for bumps, sore knees, rolled ankles, and the ride home after a hard practice.

These reusable gel packs stay flexible out of the freezer, so they can wrap around knees, ankles and other hard-to-ice spots. The included soft cover adds a barrier between the cold pack and skin, which makes it easier to use in the car or on the couch after practice.

Reusable ice packs only help if someone remembered the freezer. Instant cold packs belong in a sports bag or tournament kit for away games and minor sideline injuries.

Industry observers note that these single-use cold packs activate after folding, so parents do not need a freezer, cooler, or advance planning to get cold therapy on the sideline. They are designed to reach 32 degrees Fahrenheit, which is exactly the point.

Athletic tape is the thing nobody thinks about until someone needs it immediately. It can help with sore knees, cranky ankles, tight shoulders and small body complaints that show up five minutes before warmups.

Recent findings suggest that this 16-foot roll can be cut to size, so parents are not locked into one strip length for every kid, joint, or complaint. It is breathable, hypoallergenic, and latex-free, and it’s designed to stay on for one to three days through sweat, showers, and weather, while still allowing a range of motion.

Newly introduced shoes, wet socks, and long tournament days can turn a small hot spot into a full limp. Blister bandages take up almost no room and can save a practice, game or long ride home.

Recent findings suggest that these hydrocolloid bandages cushion blisters, cuts, and scrapes while helping protect them from water, dirt and germs. They are waterproof and designed to stay on for up to five days, which is useful when a kid’s heel is already angry and the season has no interest in pausing.

Youth sports produces scrapes, turf burns, mystery cuts, and dramatic reactions to minor blood. A small first-aid kit should have bandages, antiseptic wipes, gauze, and the basics you need before anyone starts searching the glove compartment for a napkin.

This compact hardcase packs 120 supplies, including adhesive bandages, butterfly closures, gauze pads, alcohol prep pads, antiseptic wipes, sting relief pads, gloves, tweezers, scissors, and medical tape. It is slim enough to fit in a backpack, glove box, or sports bag, but stocked well enough for the everyday cuts, scrapes, and minor injuries that come with kids playing hard.

It has been revealed that this is the most sport-specific item on the list. It matters for football, lacrosse, field hockey, basketball, martial arts, wrestling, and other sports in which player contact, falls, elbows, or sticks can impact teeth.

This boil-and-bite mouthguard molds to the teeth for a more custom fit and is made with shock-absorbing EVA material to help protect teeth, gums, and jaw during contact sports. The slim profile, airflow vents, and optional strap version make it more practical for kids who need protection but still have to breathe, talk, and keep it in place.

In a recent development, if it is not labeled, it is a donation to the lost-and-found economy. Name labels help water bottles, hoodies, towels, bags, shoes, and gear make their way back before another parent takes home the same black sweatshirt.

Industry observers note that this 114-label pack includes stick-on clothing labels, shoe labels, large and small rectangle labels, and bag tags, so parents can mark almost everything that leaves the house. The labels are peel-and-stick, waterproof and laundry-safe, which matters when the gear is sweaty, wet, washed constantly, or lost somewhere between the field and the car.

In a recent development, long practices, races, meets, and tournament days can turn kids into empty tanks fast. Energy chews are quick, portable fuel for older kids who need carbs they can eat fast without digging through a bag for whatever got crushed at the bottom.

Recent findings suggest that these chews have 23 grams of carbs per serving. They are organic, include sodium to help replenish electrolytes after exercise, and are easier to stash in a gym bag than a full-size snack.

Industry observers note that warm-up pants used to mean joggers, but kids have moved on. Wide-leg sweatpants are the more current version: loose; comfortable; and useful before practice, after practice, or on the ride home.

These have an elastic waist, pockets, and a wide-leg cut that feels more current than basic warm-ups. The fabric is lightweight, soft, breathable, and slightly stretchy, which makes these useful for school, practice, running around, and the postgame outfit change your kid suddenly cares about.

#113394. How To Give Medicine To A Child Who Refuses: Tips For Sensitive Kids

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1440 w)

How To Give Medicine To A Child Who Refuses: Tips For Sensitive Kids

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1440 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A pediatrician and a nurse practitioner share how to get medicine, saline, and bandages past kids who’d rather do anything else, plus how to handle the guilt afterward.
  • Has your child ever run around the house to avoid having their scraped-up knee cleaned and bandaged?
  • All kids are miserable when they are sick, but for children who are neurodivergent, have disabilities, and/or sensory sensitivities, symptoms can feel more intense and be more challenging to manage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A pediatrician and a nurse practitioner share how to get medicine, saline, and bandages past kids who’d rather do anything else, plus how to handle the guilt afterward.

Has your child ever run around the house to avoid having their scraped-up knee cleaned and bandaged? Does a dose of antibiotics require two adults, one to immobilize and one to administer the medication? And potentially a change of clothing for you and/or your child afterwards? If so, you might have a sensitive sick kid.

All kids are miserable when they are sick, but for children who are neurodivergent, have disabilities, and/or sensory sensitivities, symptoms can feel more intense and be more challenging to manage. And it always seems that the kids who struggle the most are the ones who will inevitably catch every bug. Unfortunately, my family is a regular fixture at our pediatrician’s office and our local CVS pharmacy as a result.

Industry observers note that medication administration is not easy for a lot of parents. And during illnesses such as the flu, strep throat, or ear infections, a whole host of medications may be recommended for pain, fever reduction, or coughs. While some of these medications are available in “kid-friendly” flavors, it doesn’t mean that your sensitive kiddo is going to agree with that assessment. Board-certified pediatrician Dr. Lauren Hughes recommends that parents choose their battles, because many medications, while helpful in ideal circumstances, aren’t critical for recovery.

Recent findings suggest that “There is no real good data for vapor rubs or OTC cough meds in kids under 6 years. Honestly, my favorite cough medicine [for] children is just a spoonful of honey,” says Hughes. “When it comes to things like ibuprofen and acetaminophen, these are helpful for controlling pain and discomfort, which can often help the child feel better so they will continue drinking and staying hydrated. However, a fever itself is not harmful in children over 60 days with normal immune systems.”.

Industry observers note that lindsay McHugh, DNP, a board-certified psychiatric mental health nurse practitioner and co-founder of Resting Roo, recommends that parents of children who have difficulty taking medications experiment with other ways to ease symptoms. “You [can] try heating packs to alleviate pain or ice packs, or if they have a stuffy, you could warm that up in the microwave, and they could hold it on a certain spot,” McHugh states, “[For fever] a warm bath or a lukewarm or even a cool bath, whatever feels right to your child at the time… to make them as comfortable as possible.”.

Both McHugh and Hughes say taking the full course of antibiotics if prescribed needs to be parents’ priority. “If we don’t take [all] the antibiotics, then they could potentially build a resistance,” claims McHugh. “If they build a resistance, then we have even sicker kids for even longer.”.

Unfortunately, antibiotics — which can taste disgusting and/or have gritty textures — can be the biggest medication battle. Hughes has the following recommendations:.

Industry observers note that an absolute game changer in our family has been my daughter learning to swallow pills. Now I wish we had tried it much sooner. McHugh says that while some 3-year-olds might be ready, parents usually can start trying with their children at age 4 or 5. “[You can start] practicing with certain foods that are somewhat pill-shaped, not too big, something soft… like a pea,” says McHugh, “[And say], ‘Let’s practice trying to not chew your pea. Let’s practice trying to swallow it.’ Practice outside of being sick. So then when they are sick, then it’s not so foreign.”.

Once my daughter got the hang of it, it changed everything: When she needed antibiotics a couple months later, the pediatrician was able to prescribe pills she could swallow.

Our entire family has a history of sensitive skin, allergies, and skin ailments like eczema. These seem to frequently coexist in individuals with other sensory sensitivities. Both my daughter and I, for example, can react to the adhesive in some Band-Aids. Now we use Band-Aids for Sensitive Skin for her or, alternatively, sensitive skin tape and non-stick gauze for protecting and healing cuts and injuries.

It has been revealed that while it’s ideal to only use products that you know your child likes and doesn’t react to, sometimes you need to make a change or try something latest for a symptom or illness you haven’t encountered before. For items with topical application, McHugh recommends checking out Environmental Working Group’s Skin Deep database to research products that may include ingredients you know your child is allergic or sensitive to or might cause a reaction.

McHugh recommends trying out upcoming topical items on an area of the body where your child is the least sensitive (which will be different for every child), while they are healthy. “Pick a 1x1 or a 2x2 inch square, and try the product, a little bit at a time. I would…see how they [and] how their skin responds,” notes McHugh, “So maybe on day two or three we do this whole leg [and] see if that’s not too overwhelming from skin sensitivity as well as the smell or feel.”.

Since my daughter and I are both sensitive to smells, I also have her smell-test products in the store aisle before we buy.

Since I have a kiddo who is sensitive to touch and texture even when she is feeling 100%, standard oral thermometers have pretty much been a no-go since she was an infant, and temporal thermometers can be tricky on a sweaty kid who doesn’t like to be touched. A no-touch forehead thermometer gets a quick read without any contact, and one with a silent mode lets you take overnight temps without waking them.

Illness can be especially tricky for younger children who can’t (or won’t) blow their noses. But Hughes says it is especially critical for infants who are under six months who are still exclusively breast- or bottle-fed: When they’re congested, they can’t breathe while feeding and are likely to become dehydrated.

For using inhalers, nasal aspirators, and nasal saline, Hughes recommends the following hold: “The adult sits down with their legs spread in a V. They put the child’s head up between their legs and then place the child’s arms under their thighs. The parent then crosses their shins/ankles over the child’s legs to hold them in place. This allows the parent to have both hands free while the child is immobilized without harming them.”.

Here are some other tips for treatment of congestion, drainage, and coughs:.

It has been revealed that illnesses and injuries can be exhausting for sensitive kids and their parents. And it can be easy to start feeling guilty for having to force your child to take medicine or do some other treatment that was uncomfortable, even if it was best for them and helped them feel better in the long term. This can be especially challenging if you are trying to teach your children about bodily autonomy and boundaries.

McHugh recommends that parents try to be clear before these moments about what you are going to have to do, that you are taking care of them, they are safe, and that you know that it may be uncomfortable, painful, or taste yucky.

According to recent reports, “[After] I would offer empathy [and] validate their experience,” notes McHugh, “And then I would say, ‘I know in the past we've talked about body autonomy, body safety. And it feels like Mommy and Daddy broke that. I’m sorry that we did that… However, we have to take care of you, and your safety is our number one priority.’”.

Recent findings suggest that when our kids are sick or have an injury, it’s a high-stress time. You’re worried about your child, but you’re also worried about doing the right thing and taking care of them the right way. And sometimes you need to do what you need to do, whether it is accepting help from those around you, asking for a break, or yes, bribing your child to cooperate with some part of their care.

Sources indicate that “When your child isn’t feeling good, you’re already on edge. It’s most appropriate to treat [them] so that they don’t get sicker, and we want to take care of our babies and do everything we can. And if it takes a couple extra popsicles…that’s perfectly okay,” reflects McHugh, “Don’t forget to take care of yourself; it’s the last thing on the list. But [sometimes] you just need a little break to go to the bathroom and cry, because it was awful.”.

#113392. 10 Times Ted Lasso Totally Nailed This Whole Parenting Thing

10 Times Ted Lasso Totally Nailed This Whole Parenting Thing

📅 15 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2071 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ted Lasso isn’t the perfect father, but he’s one who can teach us a thing...
  • Way back in 2020, when I heard that Apple TV was releasing a Ted Lasso show based on the NBC Sports English Premier League promo campaign of the same name, I dismissed the concept out of hand.
  • According to recent reports, here’s the thing I failed to anticipate: Ted Lasso is, at its core, a show about fatherhood.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ted Lasso isn’t the perfect father, but he’s one who can teach us a thing... or 10.

Way back in 2020, when I heard that Apple TV was releasing a Ted Lasso show based on the NBC Sports English Premier League promo campaign of the same name, I dismissed the concept out of hand. Sure, I loved the cheeky ads where an American football coach goes to England to manage a football club. But the premise felt too thin to flesh out into a full series, and Jason Sudeikis’ body of work up to that point didn’t inspire confidence that a sitcom based on the character could hold my attention.

I couldn’t have been more wrong.

According to recent reports, here’s the thing I failed to anticipate: Ted Lasso is, at its core, a show about fatherhood. Not in a neat, Hallmark-movie kind of way, but in the messy, long-distance, guilt-soaked, love-you-so-much-it-hurts way that a lot of us actually live it. Ted’s relationship with his son, Henry — conducted mostly through grainy FaceTime calls across a six-hour time difference — is the quiet beating heart of all three seasons.

While the rest of AFC Richmond is arguing about formations and tabloid covers, Ted is trying to figure out how to be a good dad from 4,000 miles away while working through how his relationship with his own father has formed him.

The man is not perfect. Nobody raising kids is, and running off to London without your family to accept a job you’re wholly unqualified for as an act of emotional avoidance is a narrative necessity, but it’s a flaw many folks have pointed out.

But along the way, he does his best and makes the right plays in the moments that count. And since parenting lessons wrapped inside a feel-good soccer comedy are my personal favorite delivery mechanism, let’s run through 10 times Ted Lasso gave us a genuine master class in this whole dad thing.

Recent findings suggest that it’s Ted’s first night in London. He’s jet-lagged and disoriented, and the very first thing he does is call home to Henry. He fumbles the time zones and sounds a little lost, but he makes sure his kid hears his voice before the day is out.

Recent findings suggest that there’s a version of Ted Lasso in a different corner of the multiverse who gets swept up in the new job, the new city, the chaos of it all, and phones it in on the fatherhood front. This Ted doesn’t. He knows that presence isn’t always physical. Sometimes it’s a crackling FaceTime connection at midnight your time, 6 a.m. their time, just so your kid knows you’re still there.

Henry, during a video call, asks his dad if he’s ever run into The Beatles over there in England and whether he can get a photo with John, Paul, George, and Ringo. Now, Ted knows that both John Lennon and George Harrison have been dead for decades. He also knows his kid is 8 years old and asking with complete, genuine wonder. So Ted just agrees to try. He doesn't have the heart to kill that particular joy right now.

This one is subtle, but it matters. There's a real parenting skill in knowing when the truth can wait five minutes and when it needs to be delivered immediately. Ted isn't being dishonest — he's being developmentally attuned. There's a season for everything, as a certain king once sang from the stage of a Broadway house, and this particular season called for letting a little kid's imagination breathe. Ted will level with Henry about the hard stuff — and he does, plenty of times — but he picks his moments. That's wisdom.

Sources indicate that when Michelle and Henry show up in London, Ted drops everything. They swing by the Crown and Anchor for an authentic English pub experience. They build a double-decker bus model at the kitchen table. And Henry settles into his happy place, sleeping between his parents. Even though Ted is in the midst of a brutal season, managing a locker room full of fragile egos while racking up losses, none of that matters for those few days. He is simply Dad.

Sources indicate that what makes this moment rich is what we know that Henry doesn't: His parents' marriage is already over. Michelle is about to tell Ted she wants a divorce. And yet Ted keeps the joy intact for his son. He doesn't let his own grief occupy the visit. That is an act of real parenting discipline — the ability to compartmentalize your own pain long enough to give your child a memory that isn't shadowed by yours. Most of us have had to do some version of this. It doesn't feel heroic in the moment. It just feels hard. Ted does it anyway.

Recent findings suggest that henry asks Ted why, whenever he sees him on TV coaching soccer, he never seems to be doing anything. It's a kid's question, but it's actually a perfect question. Ted's answer is one of the most quietly profound things in the entire series. He tells Henry that once the game starts, he can't really tell his players what to do — he just has to hope that everything he's been trying to teach them made some kind of dent. Then he states: “It's kind of like being a father.”.

According to recent reports, and then Henry, having absorbed none of this, is clearly already thinking about something else entirely. Ted realizes midsentence that his kid has mentally bounced. He stops talking. He smiles. He gets it. That moment is the whole job description of parenthood distilled into 30 seconds of television. You pour yourself into the role and hope it lands. You accept that you can't control the outcome. And you find a way to laugh about it — or at least smile — when your kid demonstrates, in real time, that they were not listening. Every parent reading this has lived this exact moment.

Industry observers note that henry isn’t the first kid to idolize a less-than-stellar role model, but his admiration for Jamie Tartt is a particular form of torture for Ted. As enigmatic as he is talented, Jamie makes Ted’s life incredibly difficult, even when he’s scoring goals. This puts Ted in a tough spot as Henry enthusiastically belts out the terribly annoying Baby Shark-themed Jamie Tartt song and sports his jersey with pride.

According to recent reports, but Ted lets his son revel in the moment of having access to the talented and popular starlet. He doesn’t even hint at the fact that perhaps Tartt isn’t the best guy to look up to. And when Jamie flashes Ted a smirk that makes his beautiful face even more punchable than usual while signing Henry’s jersey, Ted takes a deep breath and lets his son have a moment he’ll never forget.

Ted gets word from Michelle that Henry has been involved in a bullying situation at school — and then discovers it wasn't Henry who was bullied. Henry was the bully. Ted is shaken. And because of schedules and time zones, he has difficulty getting in touch with Henry right away.

If Ted had been around, he would likely have responded emotionally and sucked all the air out of the room. But when father and son finally get a chance to talk, Henry admits he messed up and didn't follow his dad's advice to count to 10 when he gets angry.

According to recent reports, with a little bit of forced space, Henry comes back around on his own. Ted doesn't strip his son of dignity while correcting him. And when Henry apologizes to his friend Doug with a rap in front of the class, you can almost hear Ted beaming through the phone. The lesson Ted had been repeating wasn't wasted — it just needed more time to work. Be a goldfish, sure, but also trust that the seeds you plant eventually grow. Even in the hardest soil.

Recent findings suggest that when Michelle and Henry leave London at the end of their visit, Ted walks them to the gate, knowing his marriage is essentially over and that his son doesn't know it. He says goodbye to Henry the way you say goodbye when you're not sure when you'll see each other again — fully present, holding it together, promising to talk soon. He watches Henry walk away with the airport attendant. And then the mask slips, just for a moment, and you see how much it costs him.

In a recent development, here's what Ted doesn't do: He doesn't make the goodbye about himself. He doesn't get weepy in a way that burdens Henry with having to manage his father's emotions. He saves that for after the kid is out of sight. This is something parents don't talk about enough — the emotional labor of keeping your own grief off your child's plate. It's not suppression. It's protection. There's a version of this that's emotionally avoidant and unhealthy, but Ted's version in this moment is clear-eyed and loving. He feels everything. He just knows whose feelings need managing right now.

It has been revealed that after Henry's visit to London ends and the lad heads back to Kansas, Ted does something small and wonderful. He reveals Henry, via video call, that he's placed the miniature Premier League Lego trophy Henry gave him into the Nelson Road Stadium Lego set they built together. It's a tiny thing. It's also everything.

It has been revealed that physical objects carry emotional weight for kids in ways that words sometimes can't. That Lego stadium becomes a shared artifact. It’s something Henry can picture when he thinks of his dad. Something that indicates “you were here, and you matter, and I kept a piece of what we made.”.

It's the parenting equivalent of keeping a drawing on the fridge forever. Henry even notices that Nate's Lego figure is at the back of the bench and asks about it, which gives Ted a gentle opening to explain that relationships can change without anyone being erased. Heavy stuff, delivered through the medium of tiny plastic soccer coaches.

During their Lego video call conversation, Ted tells Henry that he doesn't love the idea of being away from him and that the only reason he's staying in England is that he's doing something notable. Henry — who is, let's remember, about 10 years old — tells his dad to try to win the whole thing. Ted pushes back, saying winning isn't everything. And Henry states, essentially: “OK, but at least try.”.

Sources indicate that that's the moment a kid flips the script on you, and you realize they've been absorbing your lessons all along and also developing their own perspective on top of them. Ted doesn't dismiss the advice. He doesn't say “thanks, buddy” in that patronizing way parents sometimes do. He actually sits with it. He lets Henry be right.

Kids need to see their parents receive feedback and adjust — it's how they learn that it's a normal and healthy thing to do. Plus, Henry is objectively correct. You can care about more than winning and still bring your whole effort to the field. That's not a contradiction. That's maturity.

Industry observers note that ted walks away from AFC Richmond. He turns down the job. He gets on the plane. He comes home to Kansas and, within about 60 seconds, is coaching Henry's junior league team, running plays, completely in his element.

In a recent development, but the real parenting lesson isn't just that Ted comes home. It's why he comes home. He doesn't do it because the job went badly or because England rejected him. He does it because he looked at his life clearly and made an honest accounting of what mattered most. He demonstrated his son — showed Henry in the most concrete way possible — that he is the priority. Not in the abstract, inspirational-poster way. In the literal, I-quit-my-dream-job-in-London-to-be-at-your-soccer-games way.

Industry observers note that and then in the finale's final image, when Henry misses a shot and gets frustrated, Ted calls him over. Henry says the words Ted has been saying all series — be a goldfish — and they both smile.

The lesson came back home. Same as the dad.

#113391. Dr. Becky Kennedy on self-trust, boundaries and letting kids struggle

📅 30 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1763 w)
